utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are present. The presentation is complete as -- precisely as yesterday. The witness is present, also his counsel, Mr. Tansey. Mr. Ostojic, unless there are preliminaries, you may proceed with your cross-examination. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a pre-preliminary, Mr. President. If we could reserve perhaps two or three minutes at some point during the day just to give the Trial Chamber an idea of some scheduling for next -- next week, what we have available for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that we leave that till the very end. In the meantime, we will have seen how far advanced we would have gone with this witness. Yes, Mr. Ostojic. Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, yesterday we were speaking briefly about Dragan Mirkovic, and in order to advance the process, let me just quote what you said in several proceedings when you gave testimony before, and you tell me if that's correct or not. With respect to Dragan Mirkovic, you said on the 23rd of September, 2003, under oath, sir, that he told you that the civilian bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, could we have a transcript cite, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 1763, lines 15 through 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You testified under oath, sir, that Mr. Mirkovic told you that the civilian bodies, the civilian government requested from him to provide a vehicle so that the dead bodies of the Muslims that had been killed could be put away during the night. Do you remember giving that testimony under oath on the 23rd of September, 2003, and do you stand by it here today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by it here today, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I would like to ask you not to manipulate with what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask the Court to instruct the witness just to answer the question as he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Stop, Mr. Ostojic. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we've done really fine so far. If there is need to protect you, we will be the ones to protect you. Don't worry. We have stopped not just Mr. Ostojic but everyone else when it was needed, and we will continue to do so. So Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, one week after that sworn testimony that you stand by here today, you testified again in the Blagojevic case, and under oath again, sir, you said the following, and that's on page 2284, lines 8 through 11: "Dragan Mirkovic told me that he was personally in charge of clearing -- or, rather, transporting the bodies and digging the graves and the cleansing of the terrain as a member of the civil defence unit in Bratunac at the time." Sir, do you remember giving that testimony under oath, and do you stand by it here today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it. I also stand by the first quote you used as well as by everything I said then and what you have just quoted. In any case, I feel a need to explain that in more detail, but I shall wait with that until a better opportunity arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The third issue I want to cover with you as to no only who gave Mr. Mirkovic instructions to get a truck, who authorised him to personally supervise and to take the transportation of the Muslim bodies from Kravica to Glogova and to bury them ultimately. The third issue with respect to this I want to cover, and that's your testimony that on the 23rd of September, 2003, page 1762 for counsel, and that is all the way from lines 12 to 19. You also stated that Dragan Mirkovic informed you that between 80 and a hundred Muslims had been killed that night, meaning the night of the 13th, in Bratunac. Do you remember giving that testimony, and do you stand by that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it, and I'm ready to explain that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic should not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, when did Mr. Mirkovic tell you that he was in charge of transporting and digging the bodies of the Bosnian Muslims that were murdered at the Kravica massacre? When did he first tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise as to the time or date of that, but it was not at the time as all it was was -- all of it was happening. It was sometime later when we were discussing those matters. The war was over, and then I had an opportunity to discuss with Mirkovic those issues. We talked about the corpses, that is to say the killed people who were in Kravica. To makes things clear, I'm ready to respond to each and every of your questions, but we have to make a distinction between two things. There were those killed, and then there were those killed -- they were along the road between Sandici and Kravica and in the area of Kravica itself. That should be the first thing that is clear. Another thing what I had in mind when I confirmed what you quoted referred to a group of people that was killed after being detained in the Vuk Karadzic school, the hangar, and other buildings in that area. As regards those buildings, I refer to between 80 and 100 people and the information I got from Mr. Mirkovic to the effect that he was tasked by the Bratunac civilian authorities, that is to say the municipal president, president of the Executive Board, to have the 80 to 100 people removed once he had secured a vehicle to do so and to clean that area. Mirkovic Dragan told me that perhaps a year or even a year and a half after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let me try to put it in context. Did he tell you this before or after you personally burned the documents from the Srebrenica operation that was in your safe in May of 1996? So if we were to look at a time line, did you have this conversation with Mr. Mirkovic before or after you destroyed those documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are documents, and you have evidence of that, that the hand-over was done sometime in 1997, in March or April. I don't have that with me, so I'm not sure. In any case, that was before I handed over the documents from the vault of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But we're -- sorry, and I'll let you finish, but I'm not really interested -- and we'll get to the discussion about your destruction of documents, and with all due respect, just so you know, without being either aggressive or rude to you. It's my understanding that you burned the documents in the safe, not that you handed them over, that you set fire to them. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will talk about -- we will talk about that a little extensively in a few minutes, but all I wanted to know for this point, the time line when you had this conversation with Dragan Mirkovic, when he informed you about the burial of the bodies in Glogova, that he was in charge of it personally, both the transportation and the burial, when he told you about the 80 to a hundred Bosnian Muslims who were killed in Bratunac: When did you have this discussion with him relative to the time that you burned the documents from the safe at the Bratunac Brigade? And from my time line, that was in May of 1996 that you did that act, so when did you have this conversation with him, before or after May of 1996?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not sure about the date. We can look into a document that is in existence. That is not in dispute, the document of my hand-over. And at the same time, I did set fire to some documents. That document is in existence. I think it was in April 1997, although I'm not sure. In any case, we can refer to the document. The next thing I wanted to say is this: I did not receive any report from Dragan Mirkovic. We merely had a conversation since we were on good terms. This was no official report submitted to me by Dragan Mirkovic, and he did not brief me officially. In any case, this was after I had left the army. In any case, I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's -- let's talk about the destruction of documents for a moment. Is it true, sir, that you personally destroyed these documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I destroyed a portion of the documents from the vault of the security organ. However, it is incorrect that I destroyed any official documents kept by the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it also true, sir, that you did not receive orders from anyone to destroy those documents, and you did it on your own volition?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for counsel, you could look on page 2365 of his testimony, pages -- that was the page -- lines 10 through 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that I did not receive any orders to destroy documents, at least pertaining to those that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it also true, sir, that in May of 1996 when those documents were destroyed by you personally that you did so because you were "afraid of the consequences"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept that formulation. If I may add another sentence, there were documents which in a certain way could compromise myself and the Bratunac Brigade. I stated that openly, and there's nothing to be disputed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And those are actually, Mr. Nikolic, your words. You said, "I was afraid of the consequences," and you were afraid of the consequences because the documents that you burned, destroyed, set fire to, would compromise you personally and the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said so, and I testified to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, on the 1st of October, 2003, when the Honourable Judge Vassylenko asked you questions regarding this topic of destruction of documents or spoilation of evidence, you seemed to volunteer to him in one of your answers at page 2366, line 7, that the documents that you destroyed included your diary, your notes, and your opinions, et cetera, is the way you phrased it, and that's at line 7, counsel, 2366. Do you remember giving that testimony to the Honourable Judge Vassylenko? Do you think that's accurate as you sit here today that that's what you burned?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what other things are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also said that in the vault, there were several types of documents. It is difficult to explain in a single sentence. The first group of documents were those kept by the intelligence security organ, that is to say, myself. In the notes of hand-over, you have a list of the things contained in the vault, and you have it in groups, documents kept by the security organ pursuant to the rules of security organs, and based on that you can see that no official document of that nature was destroyed. All things that had to do with the professional expert line of work were not destroyed. I told Judge Vassylenko that I destroyed some notes, my diary, information sheets of sorts, and there is a set of documents which I kept in the vault which were information memos I received from my cooperatives in the various units without having been able to verify the information contained therein. For example, there was a mention of smuggling of arms involving two people, one on the Serb and the other on the Muslim side. When investigating, I couldn't prove those allegations. That information was in the vault. As the security organ and as required by the rules of service, I had to destroy such documents. I was under an obligation to do so. I destroyed that set of documents, as well as those which I can frankly say here were all the documents that had to do with the operation of the transfer of bodies from the primary to secondary graves. There were working notes, then there were lists of all of the participants in that operation, lists of machinery used, as well as reports on the fuel spent. I had photocopied forms that we received in the Bratunac Brigade which were in a large envelope that I was the custodian of. Those were the papers that were destroyed. Everything else, everything that falls under the title "Official documents," as you can see from the notes of the hand-over were handed over to the successor. It is all in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, isn't it also true that in May of 1996 when you set out to do this task personally without any orders to burn the documents in your safe as you've described, you did it because you knew SFOR was starting to commence searches for various documents within your brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not. I -- that was done much before I destroyed the documents. SFOR was engaged extensively in that area much earlier than the destruction of documents occurred and the hand-over. They had a base in the immediate vicinity of Bratunac. They were present round the clock working on those issues. They were visiting the field, carrying out checks. Therefore, your assertion does not stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that SFOR had nothing -- the fact that SFOR was coming to the area to search for those documents had no motivation for you to destroy those documents? Is that what you're telling us basically? Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not telling you that. I'm telling you simply that members of SFOR had already been present there. You can understand that any which way you want, but if -- if it would be favourable for you to have that as a motive, then I'll agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not a question of whether it's favourable. All I want is finally to get you to tell me the truth, and to be very frank with you, here is what you said on the 1st of October, 2003, under oath, and that's approximately --not approximately, it's page 2365. The question and your answer is long-winded, but nevertheless, you state here on lines 24 and 25: "I knew that what was underway was searches by the commands of SFOR. I took these documents, and I destroyed them." All I want to do is have you reconcile that for me, and it was my impression from reading your testimony if I accepted it ever as being truthful, and now what you say here, was SFOR really a motivating factor in addition to you being afraid of the consequences of you personally having been exposed in your brigade to what occurred in Srebrenica, or did SFOR not play a role? At the end of the day, that's all we really want to know, a final answer on this question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only normal that it did have some influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without the searches and raids ... the point is this: Why did not destroy the documents a fortnight or a month before that? I destroyed the documents on the very date of the hand-over, and it was then that the opportunity arose for me to destroy everything that I did not wish to turn over to my successor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can spend hours talking about your motives and opportunities, sir, but I just want to talk about the destruction of these documents. Isn't it true, or you tell me if it's true or false, that you destroyed all the documents relating to the period - meaning the Srebrenica operation - before the beginning of the operation, during the operation, following the operation about which you reported to the command of the Drina Corps; therefore, Mr. Nikolic, you destroyed all written documents and reports that were in your safe. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could it be? The hand-over document is there proving that it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it's true or not, but I can share with you that under oath you gave sworn testimony on the 23rd of September, 2003, at page 1773. When Mr. McCloskey, I believe, was asking you the question you gave the following answer, and that's lines 14 through 18. Mr. McCloskey, he's the Prosecutor for the Office of the Prosecution that led you in that case. On line 13: "What kind of documents did you destroy?" Answer by Mr. Nikolic, under oath, lines 14 through 18: "I destroyed all the documents relating to the period, that is, reports around Srebrenica before the beginning of operations, during the operations, following the operations about which I reported to the commander of the Drina Corps." But you don't stop. You continue, Mr. Nikolic, under oath to say the following on that same page, 1773, lines 17 through 18. You state: "Therefore, all written documents and reports that I had in my safe." That's what you said under oath six or so years ago. Can you reconcile for me or explain why you think that's not true, because in fact, Mr. Nikolic, you did destroy all the documents within the safe, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can assert whatever you like. I'm telling you what I did destroy, and I can confirm that and explain. The reports I had in the vault -- please, you don't want to stop talking, and yet you don't want me to explain. Otherwise, I'll keep completely silent. You cannot force me to say a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you don't address Mr. Ostojic. You address the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Mr. President. But if Mr. Ostojic is putting a question to me without letting me to provide an explanation, then I don't know why I'm here. Please allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead. No one is stopping you, and to my knowledge Mr. Ostojic did not try to stop you. Go ahead and finish your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is about the report that were in my safe, and they indeed referred to the period before, during, and after the Srebrenica operation. These are various reports that I kept in my safe. Basically, these reports are not to be handed over to anyone. I didn't place them in the archives, and they remained in my safe. It is true that they were inter-related and that they contained information about Srebrenica, but quite simply these kind of reports are not to be handed over to anyone because no one needed them. These are the reports that I destroyed as well as the other documents that I already mentioned. However, your claim is wrong when you say that I destroyed all the documents that were in the safe. The truth is that I destroyed the report pertaining to the relevant periods, the ones that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you gave testimony under oath and it was recorded by the court reporters in that courthouse that you said: "Therefore, all written documents and reports that I had in my safe." So I'm not surmising that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Ostojic. Now I'm going to stop you. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, what I'd like to ask you is what else was in that safe? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were pistols from war booty, some jewellery, also as part of the war booty. There was money from the war booty and official documents of the security organ that were being kept in the safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when you reference the war booty specifically with respect to the jewellery, as I think you called it spoils of war at one point, do you remember from whom specifically you obtained those spoils of war, that jewellery that was in your safe?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the items confiscated from the people who were imprisoned. They had to hand over the money, the gold, jewellery, and everything else that they had of value, and that was recorded. There was also another group of people who had been transferred from Serbia to the Bratunac Brigade, and along with them arrived the money and everything that they had, and all of that was put into the safe. At the time of the hand-over of the security organ safe, a record was made of the hand-over to the corps organ, including all the valuables that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we have that. It's reflected on Exhibit 4D687 that that occurred approximately on the 4th of April, 1997. And in particular, what I'd like to focus on are the prisoners that you received from Serbia that came, the Bosnian Muslims that you received in late or mid-July 1995. Do you remember that? You have to give a verbal answer or a -- do you remember that you received prisoners from Serbia in July of 1995, people who left the Srebrenica and Potocari area or some area there, and then they were returned back to the Bratunac Brigade, specifically to you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not returned to me. They were first returned to the border police, and that was a procedure that was a normal one at the time. A number of these Muslim prisoners who were returned from Serbia were sent to the border police. Some were handed over to the Bratunac Brigade, and then the Bratunac Brigade police, pursuant to order of the corps command, were transferred to the prisons in Knezina, Batkovici, or Vlasenica. I don't remember all of those who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How do you know they were transferred to Batkovici and Vlasenica? How do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because Zlatko Cejanovic along with the MP commander and military policeman was the person in charge of drafting the supporting documents for sending these people to these facilities. I think I saw lists from Batkovici and Knezina containing the names of these people, and it also contains information about the origin of where these people had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you consider this issue, because there's a record on the 7th of April, 1997, specifying what specific jewellery was placed in your safe, and we were able to trace that jewellery to certain Bosnian Muslims who were returned specifically to your custody from Serbia; the people on that list, sir, were you -- did you find that to be problematic for you at all with respect to your involvement in that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything problematic there because I absolutely had no other relationship apart from maintaining contact with the border police commander because he was the one who handed them over to the Bratunac police, military police -- Bratunac Brigade military police. He sometimes used to see me. I would sign a list of people who had been handed over to the Bratunac police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just quickly look, if we can, at 4D687, please. And I don't want to spend too much time on this, but I just want to highlight a couple of things for you and get your answer. And that would be page 2, but we can look at the first page, so I just want to get acquainted with the document. It's a record hand-over of documents and other material. Directing -- sir, I'm going to just quickly -- and if you do need the time, please let us know, as I'm sure you will, to read the full document. I want to focus on paragraph 20 for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and paragraph 20 talks specifically about you, sir, personally handing over to the commission certain items from the spoils of war, and then they list out six or so items, and above that they list out pistols. Do you see that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to compare some of these items to other documents that you've signed. So if you could just for this moment focus on number 1, item number 1, which is a one gold chain, and item number 3, which says "One gold men's ring," as well as item number 4, which says "four small gold -- gold chains (pierced)." So these three items in mind and then let's look at 4D431, please. And with all due respect, we're going to focus on paragraph number 4, but I'd like Mr. Nikolic to verify that that's his name that appears on the right-hand corner and that bears his signature on the copy of this document, 4D431. So, sir -- thank you. I wasn't sure --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, focusing your attention, these are some of the people that you received on the 24th of July, 1995, who were in Serbia, and then they were transferred to -- or given to the border police, and the border police transferred them to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border police transferred them to the Bratunac Brigade, and this hand-over record was signed by me on behalf of the Bratunac Brigade. Therefore, they were not handed over to me. They were handed over to the commander of the border police. He only came to my office and asked me to sign it. You have it in front of you, this list --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I said that the border police commander was also a signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to match some of the people, so if you look at item number 4, that person when he was brought to you had with him the three items that we discussed as reflected on Exhibit 4D687, and why don't you read what it says in B/C/S. If you could look, it's on the fourth line, and then we could maybe go back and match it to 4D678. What does it say on the fourth line that he had? It starts with 1, and then it says "zlatni lanac." Do you see that? So one gold chain. Can you continue reading for me? What else does it say? 1 "zlatni muski prsten," right? One gold men's ring. What else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment. Four small pierced coin, and then it says ID card number, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This individual seems to match the person whose spoils of war you had in your safe, does it not? I mean, he had one gold chain, one gold men's ring, four small gold coins pierced; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an affirmative answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- really. Please. Whose jewellery this is, I don't know. The person who arrested them or apprehended them was the one who confiscated these items and handed them over to the police with the proper record. He didn't hand them over to me. What I had in the safe was what was given to me for safekeeping --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- by the military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let's look at 4D425, please, which is another listing. Just by way of example, I wanted to see where these two people were in particular. Yes, 4D529 are also similar names of prisoners that you received from -- that were coming from Serbia that were turned over to the border and then you received them from the border, and 4D529 is actually the document that bears your signature, I believe, which identifies the balance of these spoils of war, and I really wanted to focus on these, and we want to do it in reverse this time, these three items on item -- on paragraph number 3. This person reflected on item number 3, he was bearing with him, among other things, ten gold women's rings of various sizes and one pearl necklace; correct? Do you see that under item 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we following that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. On the left-hand side, paragraph number 3, the second to the last line, it starts with ten women's gold rings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's the same -- that's the same items that are reflected on 4D687. So if we could just have 4D687, please, brought back, and that would be page 2, under paragraph 20. And just, sir, if you could look at under paragraph 20, numbers 2, which says one pearl necklace, and then number 5, which it talks specifically about ten gold women's rings of various sizes. Now, what I'm suggesting to you, sir, is that the reason you find or you should find that these people that you received problematic is because the Prosecution is alleging that these people on the list that I've showed you, that they were not transferred to Batkovici or Vlasenica but that they were killed and buried in Glogova, and you know that, and that's why in your notes, which we'll look at in a minute, you write with respect to this issue that it's problematic, and it's at that point that you start creating this story that they were transferred to Batkovici or Vlasenica. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Earlier -- you earlier told us that you didn't find it problematic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't cut him --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- like that. Although you're speaking English and he's speaking Serbo-Croat, you understand the language, and therefore, you're not allowing a pause, and you make it appear as if you are interrupting straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You continue, sir. You said, no, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. I didn't have enough time to go through all the names, but one of the names that I spotted immediately was the name of Malkic, yes, Malkic. I know this man, and I know that he is alive. He is still living and working in Srebrenica. I didn't go through all the names, but what I know and what was told me -- that is to say all the information that I had related to what happened to these people came from the MP commander and Zlatko Cejanovic. If you look at one document, you will see that it was Zlatko Cejanovic, the one who drafted supporting document and sending people where he did. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, if we could have the usher give us the original of his notes so we could direct his attention specifically to a passage within that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we are just going to take your notes for one minute and we'll return them, just so I may direct your attention to ... thank you. Yes. And this is a passage in your notes that we found, although we didn't have an opportunity to go through as closely as we would have liked. It's under the name of a person called Dragisa Jovanovic, and within, I guess, his statement or testimony, you write certain notes as you do for other witnesses where you say it's important, where you assert that the person has lied, or you find that there is a problem area, and specifically relating to these people and the issue with respect to the jewellery that was found and where those people were ultimately buried, because I'll tell you, the Prosecution, even in their update from this Investigator Janc, they find that this guy Halilovic was found in Glogova. His body was found Glogova. But I want to talk to you about this, so if you can direct your attention to this page here that's open, and towards the bottom third of that page, do you see the name Dragisa Jovanovic there, highlighted in yellow?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just to put it in context, it's not immediately -- turn the next page, sir, please. Again, towards the bottom third of that page, you'll see that there's an asterisk which says "document" in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you read that section to us all the way through and including the part where it says, "Problem."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have foreign currency --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But slowly.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in my safe, and I have pistols. I asked my commander, What shall I do with that? Based on the record, these items were --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- handed over to the chief of --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who -- the chief of who? You said you handed over to the chief.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were handed over to the chief of security of the Drina Corps. This is what it says in the statement. I am quoting from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. So this is a quote from Dragisa's statement, and we would really need to read the whole statement because these are just fractions from certain pages and taken out of context, and I would like to discuss this in this manner. These are just portions of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I have --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the full statement, and these are not complete sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's why I asked the question. If you could just help us out, sir. No one's trying to -- we're just trying to get an issue resolved here. I know that it says that, but we saw document 4D687, and we know that this Mr. Dragisa Jovanovic asserted that and you wrote it down. We know that those jewellery and all those items were not given to the chief of security of the Drina Corps, but they were given specifically to a commission. We know for sure that that commission received those items on the 4th of April, 1997. The next passage is what interests me. That's your opinion, is it not, when it starts with the word "problem," that you found this to be problematic. Those are your opinions right after that, is it not? You were nodding, but I wasn't sure ...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The first thing, I want to make it absolutely clear, what is marked with an asterisk is only a part of the statement without the full context. In order for me to discuss this, I would need to have the entire text. What you see as a problem is that I added a remark "problem" relating to where these jewellery and other items came, and it says here that they had take -- been taken over from the people who came from -- back to Serbia, and they were recorded by the MUP. It was not me who took these items from them. It was done by the commander of the military police who received them and took care of them, and also Zlatko Cejanovic who was in charge of organising the transfer of these people to prison. And it reads here they were -- the prisoners were taken from Serbia to Susica and I believe to Batkovici. And these people whose jewellery is listed here were transferred to Susica or Batkovici, so there is nothing disputable here. This is all I know about this incident. I cannot confirm with any degree of certainty how many people were where, but you can find a list of people who were in Batkovica, and you can find also the names of the people who had been transferred from Bratunac. That is all I know. Everything else was within the jurisdiction of the military police. Zlatan Cejanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the brigade command. Yes, I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you make these notes, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to explain this. These notes were a working project, so to speak. There's nothing contained here that can be taken as proof or evidence. These are not my words. These are excerpts from the statements that I was reading and my opinions about certain things. There is nothing final about this, and it doesn't reflect my ultimate position. So this was just an initial phase when I was receiving statements, reading them, thinking about what was going on. That's it. So therefore, I do not consider this document to be any valuable evidence. These are just my thoughts, and I revised my positions over the time after learning new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your long-winded answer, I failed to hear when you made these documents. Can you give me a date or a approximate date when you created them, and if you can be concise, I would personally appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This document was created in a period that is mentioned in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to repeat the answer. It was incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the interpreters didn't understand what you said. If you could kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there are three sets of notes here, the first one contains orders and statements -- or, rather, four sets with some orders, the second set contains statements of potential Muslim witnesses, and the third one is, I think, relates to international forces in Potocari, and the fourth set contains statement given by Serbian witnesses. According to the sequence of how I received them from the OTP, I analysed them and made my notes, and this is how this notebook was produced. And it contains my thoughts and preparations in order for me to be able to present to my lawyers the things that are relevant or may be irrelevant, to underline or highlight what could be crucial for my defence case, because I still didn't have the decision to enter an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were these notes, then, would it be fair to say, created prior to your ultimate plead of guilty and to those negotiations? So it was before somewhere in May of 2003; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to another topic, Mr. Nikolic. Can you tell us, sir, in 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting my friend, and I didn't want to interrupt the line of questioning, but way back on page 17, line 3, there was a mistranslation, I'm informed, something about the border police commander also being an investigator. I don't know if this is of any significance, but I just wanted to put it on record and see if my friend thought it was of significance and it needed to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It may have been a misstatement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us in 1995 in Bratunac, specifically the entire territory of Bratunac, up until the Srebrenica operation when it started, did there exist a civilian body or civilian bodies that were functioning in that area that called themselves authorities in exile?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no clue. This is the first time I hear of it. A government or authorities in exile?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah. I would have used government in exile. I'm familiar with that, but specifically authorities in exile. You're really telling us you have no idea what that is; right? Never heard of it before? I mean, that's what you said, right, just a second ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A government in exile? I don't know such a government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, help me with this, then, if you don't mind. When you, sir, on the 1st of October, 2003, gave sworn testimony in the Blagojevic case, the Honourable Judge Vassylenko asked you a question, and for my learned friend it's on page 2366, lines 15 through 17 is the question to you, Mr. Nikolic. Judge -- the Honourable Judge Vassylenko's queries: "Mr. Nikolic, can you tell us what civilian bodies have functioned in the municipality of Srebrenica at the time of the operation?" Answer by Mr. Nikolic, lines 18 through 21: "In Bratunac and in the territory of Bratunac, until the operation started there were authorities that were functioning and that called themselves the authorities in exile, and they had their offices in Bratunac, not in Srebrenica." Now, sir, you told us under oath here that you never heard of that term, but you used that term and you gave sworn testimony that you knew what authorities in exiles -- in exile is. Isn't that true? So my question to you, sir, is what you told Judge Vassylenko in 2003 false, or what is what you just uttered to this Court, that you never heard of the term "authorities in exiles," false?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to explain. In my language, it was interpreted to me as a government in exile in Bratunac. That is what heard. I was confused by that at first because there was no government in Bratunac. Next, no one could have been exiled in 1995, but had the gentleman asked me whether any representatives of the civilian authorities of -- were in the area of Bratunac, I would have said yes, there were Srebrenica civilian authorities representatives present in Bratunac. They had their offices there, although that was not their home municipality. They represented Srebrenica municipality in the territory of Bratunac municipality. They were there to represent the interests of all of the inhabitants of Srebrenica municipality. If you deem that to be exile, then it is. I'm telling you that Srebrenica authorities, representatives were in Bratunac taking care of their population in the territory of Bratunac and hailed from Srebrenica. That was the situation that was in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Focusing -- and I'm going to read it back just so we can get it correct with the translation, and they've heard your comments on that, I'm just quoting that back, and I have a question. I quote: "You stated, sir, under oath in 2003 in Bratunac and in the territory of Bratunac, until the operation started, there were authorities that were functioning and that called themselves the authorities in exile, and they had their offices in Bratunac, not in Srebrenica." All I want to do is follow up on this answer that you gave previously. When were this -- when was this group or body formed, this -- these authorities in exile, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you only approximately; sometime in May of 1992 perhaps. I am not sure of the time exactly, but it was in the period when Srebrenica fell and the Muslim forces entered. Then both the population and the authorities left the territory of Srebrenica and arrived in Bratunac in May or so. I don't know whether they established themselves as such immediately or at a certain point, but they were in Bratunac indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So this body that called themselves authorities in exile, as you recall it, started somewhere - and we're not holding you to that date - May of 1992 and lasted - would I be correct - until approximately July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know until what time they existed; probably until Srebrenica was liberated and they went back and orders were issued to establish new authorities. I would presume that up until that time they were in Bratunac and then moved to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who were its members?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some individuals, but as to the way they were elected, appointed, that I don't know, and I don't know what the authorities consisted of. Perhaps they followed the same principle as those in Bratunac. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know some of them personally, and I know they were members of those authorities, but I don't know the entire structure of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Keeping that in mind, sir, tell us who they were that you knew personally who were members of this body that considered themselves to be "authorities in exile." Like, for example, your brother-in-law Miroslav Deronjic, he was a member, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a part of their authorities between 1992 and 1995. He was supposed to establish the new authorities once they returned to Srebrenica. He was with the authorities in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You've said on page 28, line 3, that you knew some of the individuals, and then you go on to explain that you don't know exactly when they were appointed, what their job -- just name the individuals for us to the best of your recollection that you know were members from sometime in this body called "authorities in exile." Just list them for me.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to recall as many as I can: Dane Martic; Cvjetinovic, who was the municipal SDS president, I don't know his first name; Delivoje Sorak. I don't know. I really don't. Don't ask me to speculate. I know their faces, but I no longer remember the names. If I saw a list, I'd be able to tell you who they were. In any case, I enumerated those that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's switch the topic, then, because I don't want to make you any more uncomfortable than you may be answering my questions. Let's talk about the 13th of July, 1995, if you will. You gave us an overview, and I summarised it somewhat. You said from the 12th to the 13th you were the duty officer, but I remember - and you correct me if I'm wrong; these are not questions meant to mislead you or to trick you - you went to bed at about 3.00 that evening, that morning, from the 12th, 3.00 in the morning, up until the 13th, and you woke up at 7.00. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, focusing our attention from the time-period of 7.00 a.m. on the 13th, were you at the Bratunac headquarters throughout that entire day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day? The 12th or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The 13th. Thank you for asking for clarification. The 13th of July, starting from 7.00 when you awoke after having slept for four hours. The 13th, that day.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at the brigade, although I wasn't at the command all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we know that. At one point, sir, you went on the 13th to Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And also, at one point that day you went to the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road in Konjevic Polje; is that correct? And just to help you, that's when you waited 45 minutes for General Mladic to arrive. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then -- and then you came back to the Bratunac headquarters, brigade, and then after a little period of time you went back to Konjevic Polje with Mirko Jankovic and with Mile Petrovic in an APC; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you went back from Konjevic Polje back to the Bratunac headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a while, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how long? How long did it take you to drive that APC from Bratunac all the way to Konjevic Polje with Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's 20 kilometres from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I know, but -- you can do it by car, but when you do it with an APC you're going awfully slow, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is slower. We were moving more slowly, but I don't know exactly how much time --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How often --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How often would Miroslav Deronjic come to the brigade headquarters, the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not often.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he come to the brigade headquarters on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether he came -- I didn't see him, but that needn't necessarily mean that he wasn't there. In any case, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anybody ever tell you, including Miroslav Deronjic, that he went to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really -- maybe there was information to that effect, but I don't know. He may have arrived there. I heard something and -- but it was such a long time ago that I no longer remember. I did hear that he had certain problems with the telephone lines and that at a certain point he came to the brigade because of that. Whether that is true or not, I don't know. I did hear about that, but I don't know if it's correct. I was not there to greet him. I was not with him. In any case, it was supposed to have to do with the problems with the phone lines. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You told us briefly that you allegedly got instruction that the people from Potocari would be transported to be temporarily detained in Bratunac on the 12th of July, 1995. Focusing your attention on the 13th and your trips to Konjevic Polje, I know you spoke to your commander at about 9.30 in the morning on the 13th of July, Colonel Blagojevic. After going to -- after going to Potocari that first time, returning back to the Bratunac Brigade, with whom did you have any meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Mirko Jankovic and Petrovic, the commander and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- deputy commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not cutting you off, sir. I'm going to give you all the time you need to help us with this. That was the second trip to Konjevic Polje. The first thing in the morning you did, you woke up; you know that Mladic and Krstic were having a meeting. You had a meeting about Blagojevic at 9.30. You head off to Potocari, and then you come back to the Bratunac Brigade, and then from the Bratunac Brigade you go to Konjevic Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just sticking with at that period, and just so we're clear, the meeting you're talking about with Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petrovic that was the second time you went to Konjevic Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's stick with the first one for now, and we'll reach the second one hopefully. During this first time that you went to Konjevic Polje, who instructed you to go to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one instructed me in particular. I simply learned that during that day, perhaps an hour or an hour and a half after -- later, General Mladic was supposed to travel along that route. Together with a military policeman, I got in a car and went there to check the safety of that road. There were no particular instructions. I simply thought that that would fall under my regular tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So up until this point, immediately upon leaving Bratunac headquarters to go to Konjevic Polje, no one gave you the instruction to do that. Did anyone instruct you to advise the people at Konjevic Polje that they should transport the Bosnian Muslims that were detained to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether anyone told me or ordered me to, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the first time you decided to inform someone to transfer the detained Bosnian Muslims from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac was when you would reach the MUP check-point upon your arrival at the Konjevic Polje crossroads?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When -- when did you first make the decision unilaterally to transfer Bosnian Muslims who were detained in Konjevic Polje to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I want to say that that was not done unilaterally. On the 12th already, the places where those detained were supposed to be kept were known. On the 12th, in the afternoon, by that time there had already been some detainees at the Vuk Karadzic school. As the security intelligence organ, I was, among other things, to a certain extent - since I wasn't alone in that, but I'm talking about my responsibility - I was tasked with transferring those detainees to the place where a number of Muslim men had already been kept. As I said in my initial testimony, for a while I had contact with Dusko Jevic. He was he that I told to the first time that if there were any detainees, any captured, that they should be transferred to the locations where there already were some detainees, and those facilities were being secured. I believe I listed them before. Of course, never did I dream of what the actual figures of detainees will be. I did expect some, but not hundreds and up to a thousand. I didn't know that would happen. This was not done of my own accord. It was no decision of me alone. Simply, all of those who were detained and separated were being brought there. I don't know see anything illogical about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. You said here in your answer at page 33 that you had contact with Dusko Jevic, and it was he that I told for the first time, et cetera. Just so I'm clear, sir, and help me with this, are you saying that the first person you told that they should transfer the Bosnian Muslims who were detained in Konjevic Polje to Bratunac was Dusko Jevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where did you have this meeting with him? At the MUP check-point at Konjevic Polje, at any other place, Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dusko Jevic was in Potocari, not along the route you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of his unit were engaged in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So let's go back and just try to clarify this a little. The morning of the 13th, 1995, you go from Bratunac headquarters to Potocari, you meet Dusko Jevic, and there you tell him, what, that the detainees from Konjevic Polje should be transferred to the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked, and among other things Dusko Jevic said -- well, we were talking about things in general. In any case, he said that part of his unit or the unit he belonged to was along that road. There were no orders or instructions. I wasn't in any position to order or instruct Jevic. It was just a conversation in which I told him that all those who would surrender or be detained along that route should be sent to Bratunac. That was my comment, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I want to focus on. Your comment -- from whom did you learn that "all those who would surrender or be detained along that route should be sent to Bratunac?" From whom did you gather that information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a well-known thing, sir. Everyone knew where detainees should be sent to, at least as the AOR of the Bratunac Brigade is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you, sir, instruct the MUP at the check-point of Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road to send the detainees that were captured to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I arrived there and saw that there were those captured, I told the members of the MUP there that transport should be organised and the detained taken to Bratunac. If we are talking about my first departure there, at that time there was a smaller group of detainees. There were not many detainees in Konjevic Polje itself. In any case, I did say to the MUP members that they should transport those detainees to Bratunac. In any case, there were very few of them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: True or false, Mr. Nikolic: When you met Dusko Jevic, did you tell him to pass an order to his units which were on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje that all the captured Muslims on this road be transported to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. I told him that if he was in contact with all units that may have some detainees, that those detainees can be transferred to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I said to pass an order. From whom did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe there was a written order, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, I only think -- because I think the translation was wrong, I don't think -- and I can help you -- sir, I think the translation is wrong. That's the only reason I'm interrupt -- they said that maybe there was an order, but I think you were trying to say something else, with all due respect, but if you could start from the beginning, and I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You were talking about me conveying an order. I told you what I said, Dusko Jevic. I may have said something to that effect, but neither then nor now do I believe I could order Dusko Jevic anything. It was simply an information as to what to do with the captured, and this was the normal way of communicating. I did not receive any order from anyone what to do. Nobody told me, Nikolic, you are to convey this to Dusko Jevic. I simply encountered him, and I thought it necessary to tell him that. I didn't know that by that time he had some captured, and I simply told him that they should be transferred to the area previously designated for their Assembly. I believe this was a normal way of communicating between two people working on the same task.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived in Konjevic Polje, did you give instructions or direct the people there to transport the Bratunac men -- I'm sorry, the Bosnian Muslim men to Bratunac? Did you give instructions, and did you direct them to do so?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you believe that it falls under instructions, the thing I told them that the detainees have to be sent to Bratunac, then I can accept that. The people I knew there, I told them that the captured that they had can be transferred to Bratunac. Objectively speaking, in Konjevic Polje, in my knowledge there were not sufficient forces or facilities that can be used to secure and keep prisoners. That's why I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, just quickly, if I can ask you before the break, do you remember approximately or specifically, if you do, what time you returned to the Bratunac headquarters after your second trip to Konjevic Polje with the APC where you shared with us the story of being with Mirko Jankovic or -- yeah, Mirko Jankovic and Mile Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back in the afternoon. What I remember best would be that that took place between 5.00, 5.30, 5.45, and 6.00 p.m. Please don't hold me to it because it was long ago. Let's say between 5.00 and 6.00 on the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One couple -- one last question before the break, sir. From 5.00 up to 8.00 or let's say even 10.00, were you at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters for that entire period of time? Or you tell me. I'm sorry. Let me restate the question. From 5.00 or 6.00 when you claim you returned to the Bratunac headquarters, how long did you stay at the Bratunac headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between one and a half hours, two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just to clear this up. After that one and a half two hours, where did you go? Where's the next place you went?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere until I received a call. I was at the brigade command throughout the whole time until I received the call.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the call that you alleged happened from the communications centre in which you were summoned to go see Mr. Beara in the centre of Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you. Its think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so too. How much longer do you have, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to estimate. I've really taken out quite a bit. Sorry. I think an hour if I can have the Court's indulgence on that. I'm not sure how long I've gone so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In my mind I would be very reluctant, but we'll check how long you've been, and we'll come back to you after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know you're going to offer an opinion or give your instructions to my friend as to the amount of time he may have, and just in advance of that, I thought I would let you know that we will not be using three to four hours. I would expect a realistic estimate at this stage is inside of two hours unless something unforeseen happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It doesn't really make a difference in our mind. Mr. Ostojic had asked -- we had given each one of you two hours. Mr. Ostojic asked for three. We are prepared, of course, to grant him the three hours. You've been already two hours and 24 minutes. Try to stick to the three hours. If there are a few leftovers and it doesn't involve much more time, we'll try and consider extending it, but try to finish in three hours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about the issue relating to this purported call that you received to go and see Mr. Beara at the centre of town on the 13th, but I had -- in my haste in getting to that topic, I omitted to ask you another question which I'll go back to, and then we'll come back to this topic that you've alleged. Now, you said on page 35, lines 4 through 6, and we were talking at that point, just to put it in context for you, how is it that you were going to Potocari and Konjevic Polje on two occasions talking to the MUP at the check-point then the MUP officers at Konjevic Polje to transfer the detained Bosnian Muslims to Bratunac, and in essence and I know what you've said, and I'm not saying you didn't say other things. You've said: "Everyone knew where detainees should be sent to at least as the AOR of the Bratunac Brigade is concerned."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that there's an intercept that the Prosecution had in its possession which they've declared was exculpatory under Rule 68 where they capture Mr. Beara on the 13th of July, 1995, in essence telling people that the detainees from Nova Kasaba should be transferred to Batkovici? Do you know about that intercept?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn back now to the 13th of July, 1995, and this evening -- purported communication that you received. At any time that evening prior to receiving that communication was Mr. Miroslav Deronjic at the Bratunac headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Mr. Deronjic. A short while ago, I said that I hadn't seen him. I didn't have any communication with him. Whether he was there or not, I don't know. I want to make myself quite clear. The fact that I didn't see him doesn't mean that he wasn't at the command of the Bratunac Brigade, but I myself didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Up until that point in time, meaning when you were at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters before you received this purported call from the communications centre, did you know that there was going to be a transfer of Bosnian Muslims held in Bratunac to another place and/or to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was the code-name for the Bratunac headquarters telecommunications centre? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Badem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we think so, too, but I thought you would know more concretely than that. Yes, it was Badem. Now if we could look at Exhibit P1149A and B, B being the B/C/S version which is typed out and A being the English version. And as this is coming up, sir, my first question in this regard, have you ever seen this intercept before or this document that identifies a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you until I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're trying to get it up. Let me move to another area, and we can come back to this in brief order as long as I get a signal that we've found it. Okay. Sir, they're trying to get the document, and we could show it to you. I have a copy, but it has some markings on it. If it doesn't work, we'll use my original copy. Now, in 2004 you gave an answer to questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's coming. One moment. Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. And I apologise for the interruption, but there was a technical hitch, which I think in the meantime has been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, before -- can I ask you, what time was this purported meeting or encounter with Mr. Beara at the centre of Bratunac on the 13th of July, 1995? And in various testimony, I'll just try to remind you or refresh your recollection, you said it happened at approximately 8.30 p.m.; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said between 1500 hours and 8.30, and I really don't remember exactly. I gave you a rough timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In all your prior testimonies, you've concretely said that it was approximately 8.30. Do you stand by that, or do you think that now it was from 1500 hours --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But let's focus on this exhibit which we have in front of us which is -- purports to be an intercept that was captured on or about July 13th, 1995. On the top, sir, there's a certain frequency and channel and a time, and then it talks about the participants, and do you see the name Badem there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you agree as you sit here that that's the Bratunac Brigade headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this is a conversation that apparently was between Mr. Deronjic and Dr. Karadzic and actually an intermediary with Dr. Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Had you seen this document ever before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now do you remember reading this document and learning that it was Dr. Karadzic and Deronjic who decided that the Bosnian Muslims from Bratunac should be moved?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't exactly deduce that they made that decision at that point exactly, but they did talk about the prisoners detained in Bratunac and about their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You told us, I think, in your testimony on Tuesday that at this 12.00 or 12.30 midnight meeting that you allege that you participated in with Deronjic that he was insisting at that point that the Bosnian Muslims from Bratunac be transferred to Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was insisting on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your understanding and recollection, from 8.10 - which is the time that this conversation was captured - up until this alleged meeting that you attended at 12.00, 12.30 p.m. on the same day, given that Mr. Deronjic was insisting that the Bosnian Muslim prisoners in Bratunac be transferred to Zvornik, when did you learn that information for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that the prisoners should be transferred from Bratunac to Zvornik, and that is what I heard for the first time from Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, according to the document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he mentioned Mr. Deronjic, but I stand to be corrected if that's not the case. You heard the information that the prisoners should be transferred from Bratunac to Zvornik the first time from Mr. Deronjic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I said. Or maybe I did. No, no. I said Colonel Beara, from Colonel Beara. If I -- if I said Colonel Beara, then it was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you need to clarify this. The question was as follows: To the best of your understanding, Mr. Nikolic, and recollection, from 8.10, which was the time this conversation was captured up until this alleged meeting that you said continued at 12.30 on the same day, given that Mr. Deronjic was insisting the Bosnian Muslim prisoners in Bratunac be transferred to Zvornik, when did you learn that information for the first time? And you answered, according to the transcript, which you are free to correct, you answered: "... information that the prisoners should be transferred from Bratunac to Zvornik, and that is what I heard for the first time from Mr. Deronjic." Is this what you said, and is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After the meeting with Mr. Beara. That's how I understood it, and that's why I responded in that way. So after the meeting with Mr. Beara and in that period between 20.30 when I met Mr. Beara and the next meeting which took place on the premises of the SDS the same evening, the truth is that I heard from Mr. Deronjic for the first time that he insisted that all the detainees be transferred to Zvornik. However, before the SDS meeting, I met with Colonel Beara, and it was from him that I heard that the prisoners from Bratunac should be transferred to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Our position -- is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's clear enough if this is what he maintains, but in my mind there are questions, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There are many. But I think we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I tried to clarify what the question is because previously, I don't know who was asking you the question, or in your statement -- in your statement attached to your -- related to your plea agreement, you had -- you had told us that there was a meeting between Beara and Deronjic. You were present nearby. You're not taking part in the meeting yourself, but you were present nearby and you could hear the conversation, and you said that initially there was quite a heated argument between the two, the argument being that Deronjic didn't want the prisoners to be transferred to Bratunac or remain in Bratunac while Beara seemed to be taking that position that they be kept and they be taken to Bratunac in the first place. What you have just answered seems to me to be exactly the opposite, because what you said a minute ago, line 7 on the previous page, page 44: Yes. After the meeting with Mr. Beara. That's how I understood it, and that's why I responded in that way. So after the meeting with Mr. Beara and in that period between 20.30 when I met Mr. Beara and the next meeting which took place on the premises of the SDS the same evening, the truth is I heard Mr. Deronjic for the first time that he insisted that all detainees be transferred to Zvornik.
