However, before the SDS meeting I met with Colonel Beara, and it was from him at that I heard that the prisoners from Bratunac would be transferred to Zvornik." In other words, at the end of this last meeting, do I take it that Mr. Beara agrees, as well, that the prisoners be transferred to Zvornik or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. This is what you need to -- since there are two meetings, you need to clarify exactly what the position obtained at the very -- the occasion of the last meeting when you met with Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The final position regarding the detainees and what I heard at the meeting after the discussion was that all the prisoners should be transferred as quickly as possible from Bratunac, and I explained the reasons for this position, and the reason was because there were thousands of people in Bratunac, in the streets, in the buses, in trucks. The school was crowded. Some people were taken off the buses and killed. Therefore, there were no conditions to provide security for them in Bratunac due to this complete chaos that prevailed there, and ultimately all those who took part in the meeting and who were engaged in this operation decided to transfer them as quickly as possible towards Zvornik or to the facilities located in the area of responsibilities of the Zvornik Brigade. Your Honours, let me just say one more thing. There was so many illogical things. There was so much confusion, all kinds of decisions, arguments, misunderstandings and the like. And believe me, if I make a mistake, I'm really sorry because it is difficult for me to follow all this. I'm only trying to forget all this because I really had enough, and I'm finding it hard to do what I'm doing here today. And if I give you a wrong time or a wrong date, please understand that I am also pretty tired. I will do my best to provide this testimony in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if I could just follow up on some of what you said, although I agree with the Court that it does seem somewhat inconsistent, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't say inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I hope you are sincerely sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought you said inconsistent, but let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: I think the Court was trying to ask you on Tuesday, sir, that if you're right and if what you're telling us is the truth, that you had this meeting with Mr. Beara in the centre of town and that he instructed you or told you or informed you that the Bosnian Muslims from Bratunac were going to be transferred to Zvornik, then if you're also telling us the truth - which we dispute, respectfully - that you were at this meeting being at or near or by this meeting, depends on which of your prior testimonies we're going to stick with, with Deronjic and purportedly Mr. Beara in the SDS meeting, and then Mr. Deronjic wanted the prisoners from Bratunac to be transferred to Zvornik, yet you also add in there that Deronjic and purportedly Mr. Beara were in a heated argument as to where the Bosnian Muslims should be transferred to. Don't you find that somewhat illogical if what you're saying in some instances is true, that Mr. Beara allegedly wanted the Bosnian Muslims transferred to Zvornik, Mr. Deronjic wanted the Bosnian Muslims transferred to Zvornik, yet they were arguing and had a heated discussion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be glad to respond. The situation that prevailed on the 11th, 12th, and the 13th, could you really believe that you could have consistent decisions about something that is totally in order and that all the orders were clear and consistent? It was obvious that the decisions, what to do and how to do things were changed and made every ten minutes, as far as I know. Instructions were pouring in. Orders were pouring in. Of course, I'm not talking about written instructions, but there were telephone calls. There were communications through radio communication lines, and there was a huge influx of information that affected the positions and the decisions on what to do next. I was trying to describe to you the situation in Bratunac. There were thousands of people on the streets of Bratunac. They had been brought in there from that axis, and the people who were supposed to secure them had left, simply left. The battalions of the Bratunac Brigade were dissolved. Everybody went home. Nobody listened to anyone. The same situation prevailed when it came to taking a decision what to do with these people, regardless of the fact that there were many people from the army, from the -- both civilian and army police, from the reserve forces or people who were under work obligation, including civilians armed with rifles. The situation was horrible. And as for the status of these prisoners, they made different decisions every half an hour, let's say. Decisions were made as to what to do with them, who was going to secure them, et cetera. I know that in that context there are some illogical aspects. In one evening -- in one meeting, Mr. Beara wanted them to -- these illogical aspects derived from the previous decisions. I am trying to do my best and to help you -- help us all get at the truth and that you get the picture of the situation that prevailed in Bratunac at the time. I know it is very easy in hindsight to say what should have done and what should have been done according to the law, but that is not what was happening in reality. The situation was totally out of control in Bratunac, in all aspects. I tried to explain to you why and how these illogical aspects appear. I am sorry if I didn't manage to explain this in the best possible way and sorry for being such -- sorry for giving you such a long answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I would like the witness to repeat what he said after he said, I know in that aspect there were some illogical aspects. The witness said: "In one evening -- in one meeting, Mr. Beara wanted them to --" and we see some dots. Mr. Momir Nikolic, what did you say in that context? "In one evening -- in one meeting, Mr. Beara wanted them to --" After that, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, and I stand by it, is as follows: My first conversation with Mr. Beara took place in the centre of the town. On that occasion, Mr. Beara conveyed an order for me for all the prisoners in Bratunac to be transferred to Zvornik. What happened afterwards, I can explain. On that same day, that is the 13th, when I returned from Zvornik, another meeting was held where I was present and heard what was being said. In this meeting, Mr. Beara told Mr. Miroslav Deronjic that he had instructions for the prisoners to stay in Bratunac. Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, in this second meeting, insisted that all the prisoners should go to the territory of Bratunac as soon as possible. Everything else I can explain further, of course, if I'm asked to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you described the situation in Bratunac in the evening of July 13th, 1995, as being terrible, thousands of people there. You've also described it in other testimony that it was chaotic. It was highly stressful. There were people everywhere within the town. Is that accurate still today in your memory?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said then is something I can explain in detail further, but in principle that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And basically, you said that you wanted us to get the picture, and the picture that you would draw, if permitted - and we will permit you to do that - is that the situation in the town of Bratunac was, as we've said, chaotic. And I know you could draw other examples from it, but it was a pretty crazy situation at that time, wasn't it? And we're talking about July 13th, 1995, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was disorder, and I agree with you. We can absolutely call it chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you called it that, so let's stick with that if you don't mind. Now, sir, are you telling us that you want us to believe that you went in the centre of town during this most chaotic period when there were people going all over the place, thousands of prisoners, various people, that you met Mr. Beara in the centre of town alone, allegedly at 8.30?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned the chaos, I had in mind the evening of the 13th of July and that night, the whole night. I was then discussing the general situation. However, that was not the same situation that we had at 8.00 p.m. There were convoys of prisoners coming in during the night, on a large scale. The situation was chaotic in terms of security of prisoners, new buses arriving, et cetera. As for the town of Bratunac, it's a small town with one hotel with one main road, one Assembly building, the MUP building, and a few houses. It wasn't difficult to find anyone if you wanted to in the centre of town. It's no New York. There's only one main street. As soon as you leave any of the buildings that I mentioned, you are in the centre of town. I claim absolutely that you could find anyone if they wanted to be found in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Describe for us what Mr. Beara looked like at this purported meeting in July 13th at 8.00 or 8.30 of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know Mr. Beara very well. If you're asking me to describe his appearance then, I can tell you that he looked pretty much like any other person in uniform, but this was an officer whom I knew excellently well. Countless times did he come to see me in his official capacity to Bratunac, and there's no need for me to describe him because I know him very well. We sat together numerous times, and I can also tell you that I hold him in high regard as a person. Mr. Beara, as any other soldier in uniform -- well, that's how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Here's what you told Peter McCloskey, the OTP Prosecutor, on page 1743, lines 2 through 6. He asked you: "Had you had any contact with Colonel Beara before meeting him that night in the centre of town on this day or the day before?" Answer: "No, I never had any contacts with him previously, but I did see him once, I believe on the 13th, in Bratunac, but up to that point I had not been in personal contact with Colonel Beara, no." Do you stand by that sworn testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it. I still claim that I did not see Colonel Beara in the course of those few days in Bratunac. We did not have any contact in Bratunac during those few days. In any case, there were so many officers from the Main Staff with whom I did not have any contact, and yet they were in Bratunac. If you want me to be precise, given that you were invoking my notes -- yes, yes, you did. You used that as arguments, trying to claim something of it was true or not. In great many statements, one can read that Mr. Beara was in Bratunac even before that time. I don't know if that was the case. I only know that I did not see him. I did not have any contact with him in the course of those few days except for the 13th. As for whether he was here without me seeing him, of course there is that possibility. There were many others who were there, but I didn't see them or have contact with. If you're asking me what I believe, I can tell you that I believe Colonel Beara was in Bratunac before the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, let's focus on the second meeting. You're aware -- that's the one at about 12.30 or so at the SDS building where allegedly you were near the offices of Mr. Deronjic with this purported conversation that you overheard took place. You're familiar, are you not, that Mr. Deronjic, during your sentencing hearing, that he acknowledged that not only could he not remember you, but he said that you were not at this meeting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still claim that I was not in that meeting. I remember, and I stand by what I said, that I was not one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You just happened to be in the next room overhearing the conversations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Mr. Beara asked me to take him to the SDS office, and I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you make an introduction of Mr. Beara to Mr. Deronjic allegedly?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had known each other before that. In any case, I said that that was Colonel Beara, my boss, as I used to refer to him, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having a meeting with Mr. Deronjic here at the United Nations Detention Unit where he confronted you about your alleged involvement or participation in this meeting in December of 2003 and going into January 2004? Do you remember that he confronted you and said, Look, I gave evidence. I couldn't remember that you were there, and I told the Prosecution you weren't there, and I don't believe that you were there. Why did you come up with this telling me and telling the Prosecution that you were at that meeting? Do you remember having that conversation with Mr. Deronjic at any time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I had countless conversations with Deronjic. As to what he said about us discussing, I really cannot comment on that. We discussed many issues. I would have preferred not to have been anywhere near there, including that meeting. I would be the happiest man without being present at any of the meetings, including the one of the 13th. I was, however, and as far as I recall Mr. Deronjic confirmed in his testimony that I was in the offices but did not participate in the meeting. That's what I can recall concerning Deronjic's testimony in my case on this and including this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but isn't it true that you told Deronjic that you weren't there and that you supposedly learned about this meeting allegedly from Mr. Beara at a later time? Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, and I don't think I ever said anything to that effect. I truly do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see -- let's see if Mr. Deronjic has it right or if you do or neither of you do. If we could have P3139 on the e-court, please. And this, sir, was during a closed session that Miroslav Deronjic gave evidence on in the Blagojevic case, and at that point he's conveying with Mr. McCloskey leading the charge because he was given that information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was at that point, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It remains closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought they released it and it's open, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's the 19th of January, 2004, pages 6138 and onward.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm looking at the transcripts right now. I'm trying to find that exact site, but my information is that this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic himself concedes that it was in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it says so on the first page of this, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing it out to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm trying to confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can explain, I think, and it was because it was during the same time that Mr. Deronjic pled guilty, and they were actually having some difficulty as to what portion should or should not be open at that point as it may relate to Mr. Nikolic, I believe. But I think it's all okay to be in public session now, but I'll proceed as the Court instructs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you that it's all okay. You're jumping to conclusions. I just want to make sure whether it's still a protected piece of evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is open session. It has been -- it has been opened. That portion has been opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if we could have P31 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's fine now. In the transcript, it says 1335 and 1339. That's why we have the wrong document on the screen, but I believe my learned friend will correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Then check that again, Mr. Thayer, and let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's P3139, and we've I think put in a couple of pages of that, and if you could turn to page 6 of that document, please, which is in the official trial transcript dated 19th January, 2004, page 6138. Just so the Court can see -- page 6138. So the next two pages, please. And towards the bottom on line 22, this is where it begins on closed session, and if we can turn kindly to the next page. And I'm going to focus our attention on line 16 through 18 of that page where Mr. Deronjic on being questioned by Mr. McCloskey says: "I was supposed to testify in detail about the presence of Mr. Nikolic at that meeting. During my testimony at the time, I said -- I reiterated my position that I did not recall whether Mr. Nikolic was present at that meeting or not, but I did leave a theoretical possibility, more in the sphere of theory, that perhaps he could have been present, but I did not register that or remember that. Of course I was aware of the gravity of my testimony, and I believe that that testimony had certain implications in other cases ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The next page, Mr. Nikolic, for us to focus on really begins at the top, and that's where Mr. Deronjic says that he met with you at the UNDU on an occasion during either Christmas or New Year's, and he essentially had a conversation with you about this fact which he disputed. And it goes on to say, and we can all read it from lines 11 and onward or from lines 1 to 23, but I want to focus it in the interest of time, he says at line 10: "And I told him that I would like to know the truth, that I believe that it is very important, and I did not want to have the feeling that I had said something that was not right. And he ..." meaning you, Mr. Nikolic, "... responded at that point ..." Then Mr. Deronjic goes on to say: "I will try to quote him ..." you, Mr. Nikolic, "... as much as be. He ..." meaning you, Mr. Nikolic, "... said: Well, I wasn't there. I wasn't present in the office. I was really confused. I said ..." meaning Mr. Deronjic, "... so how could you have talked about the conversation that was conducted at the office, and he said ..." meaning you, Mr. Nikolic, "... that the details and the gist of that conversation he ..." meaning you, Mr. Nikolic, "... learned directly from Mr. Beara." And it goes on, and we can give that to you, which I'm sure you've reviewed because in October and September 2007 you were given all these materials to look at and review in preparation for your testimony. Is Mr. Deronjic being truthful here? Did you meet with him, first of all, at Christmas, New Year's at the UNDU from 2003/2004 period?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I claim, that the fact that I wasn't there is not true, everything else concerning Mr. Momir [as interpreted] Deronjic said. It's not something that I can offer any comment on as to what he thinks of that meeting. I state that I was in the offices of the SDS when the meeting was taking place and that I heard what the participants said. That's what I assert. I know what it was they discussed. I know how the meeting developed, and I know the details to the extent I could overhear. I have already testified about that, and I'm ready to repeat everything I previously said concerning that meeting. I also wanted to say another thing. Mr. Deronjic, Miroslav, that evening, as well as your client - I'm sorry to have to say this - both of them were drunk. They were not aware of the things they were saying or doing. I'm sorry to have to say this, but I have to. You want me -- you want to picture me as a person with amnesia. Deronjic and your client in particular was drunk. He had no idea what he was doing. It wasn't the first time round. It was the 50th time round. Whenever I saw him, he was drunk. I can put my life on it and say -- when I say that I was there. I overheard the discussion. I can repeat that. It was ugly, abusive. When the whole thing was over, they sat down and continued discussing things much more calmly, and again, they had a drink, both. I know everything they said at the meeting. I know the details, and I know what followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say that Mr. Beara was drunk every time that you saw him allegedly. Was he also drunk according to you, sir? I don't -- you said something, and I didn't want to cut you off. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, pardon me? I didn't hear what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought I heard you say "slazem se," that you agreed up to that point to it. But in any event, my question is you say that Mr. Beara was drunk --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You say that Mr. Beara was drunk every time that you saw him, allegedly. Was he also drunk, sir, when you claim that you saw him at 8.30 in the centre of town during the chaotic period in Bratunac on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was always inebriated, drunk to a point. He was always semi-drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is that a yes to my question that at 8.30 on the 13th of July in the centre of town, Mr. Beara was drunk?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not stating that. I wasn't trying to analyse him in the two minutes while he was giving me the task. At this meeting, however, where I was, he was very tipsy, drunk, actually, both he and Nikolic [as interpreted]. After they had that fight, they finally sat down and started talking more calmly but having a drink alongside that. When I saw him prior to that, I did not try to analyse him. There was no time. He simply said what he had. I left to do it, and that's it. I'm not stating that he was drunk at 7.30 or 8.00 when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to be fair to one of our accused as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Line 24, "Nikolic" should read "Deronjic."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's just be fair about this for one moment. You're now moving the time-frame that you saw Mr. Beara purportedly in the centre of Bratunac. Consistently when you've given testimony before you've already said it was 8.30. Now you said maybe 8.00 to 8.30. Now you've kind of moved it to 7.30, 8.00. As you sit here, can we finally have your best recollection as to when you claim you saw Mr. Beara in Bratunac in the centre of the town on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying not to assert that I know what the exact time was because I don't know. No one would be capable in such a pace of events to tell you whether something took place half an hour earlier or later. No one could do that. In my view, it is more important what happened or whether it happened 30 minutes before or later. That's why I'm intentionally not being that precise because I simply don't know what the time was. However, I'm trying to picture the event the way I saw it. I stand by what I said. I'm not certain about the time. It could have been half an hour, three-quarters of an hour before that, or ten minutes later. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's why I was trying to place it in a time-frame for you, if it was before or after this conversation that Mr. Deronjic had with Dr. Karadzic and his intermediary at 8.10 or 20.10 hundred hours on the 13th of July, 1995. But be that as it may, in the -- when you gave answers to the commission in 2004, your handwritten answers, you write on -- with respect to paragraph 5 or question 5 the following, among other things. I want to read it to you. I want to see if you still stand by it: "The civilian authorities ..." Maybe I should just -- it's on Exhibit P4477. Thank you. It's on page 7 of that document, answer to question number 5. In part, you say: "The civilian authorities played a special and central role in the planning, decision-making, and organisation of the forces -- of the forced relocation of the civilians from Potocari to the Muslim-controlled territory Kladanj. Their decisive role in this phase was manifested from the top, from President Karadzic via Miroslav Deronjic, the civilian affairs commissioner who was appointed to that post on Karadzic's personal order and the representatives -- representatives of the judicial and executive authorities of the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities. The authorisation and tasks of Commissioner Deronjic and the civilian authorities can be seen in Karadzic's orders, which exist as evidence." There's more to the answer, but I want to focus on this paragraph now, just to be fair. Do you remember saying that, sir, and writing that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So when you say they played a special and central role, what do you mean, that the civilian authorities played a special and central role?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. The information I have is the following: The civilian authorities, including Miroslav Deronjic, as SDS president and commissioner appointed by Mr. Karadzic; then Srbislav Davidovic who was president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac; then Mr. Simic as the Assembly speaker of Bratunac; then Miodrag Josipovic and Dragomir Vasic. You'll ask me why I include these two in the civilian structures. In my deep belief and what I'm certain of is that members of the civilian structures, including Miroslav Deronjic, were the ones who had it under control and regulated everything concerning the engagement of the military police, and they did that with Mr. Miodrag Josipovic. Their participation [Realtime transcript read in error, "partial"] and influence at such meetings and everything that resulted from the authorities Mr. Deronjic had based on his appointment as commissioner in and of itself provided Deronjic with a lot of authority, and from that position he could even use force, police force if anything needed to be done, regulated, or requested, and this also entails the use of military force to resolve a problem. Therefore, his influence was great. There were the armed forces there, and I have in mind the officers of the Main Staff and the corps command, because they jointly participated in the making of all decisions concerning the status of detainees, civilians, and all those in the territory of Bratunac municipality. That is that in brief, and I still claim that Miroslav Deronjic, the civilian authorities, and those belonging to them had great influence and that to a large extent they influenced the decisions that went through Miroslav Deronjic up to President Karadzic and the other way around. That is what I think, and I'm certain that they participated in the meetings and arrangements having to do with the status of detainees, and there are, of course, documents that can corroborate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to correct the transcript. On page 61, line 10, the first word is "partial," and the witness was talking about participation, participation of these people to the meetings, and it wasn't "partial."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, also you state that Miroslav Deronjic was the superior officer of the Zvornik CJB, public security centre; senior officer, Dragomir Vasic. Is that correct? And it's on page 8 of the exhibit that we're discussing, P4477.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps this is not a very happy solution and wording because it doesn't reflect what I actually thought. What I think is that during that period, Miroslav Deronjic, as the commissioner entrusted with the organisation of civilian authorities in Srebrenica on the authority of the president, and Mr. Vasic was in charge of setting up police forces in the newly liberated municipality, that led me to believe that Mr. Deronjic was superior to Mr. Vasic because setting up of civilian authorities was within the remit of Mr. Deronjic. And when it comes to command or military terms, I don't think that he was a superior officer to Mr. Vasic in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, neither were in the military at that point, I believe, but nonetheless, do you remember that there was a meeting at approximately 8.30 on July 13th, 1995, between Vasic and Mirkovic to discuss the removal of the Bosnian Muslims who were murdered at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if we are referring to the same things. If not, then please correct me. What I know is that sometime on the 13th this meeting took place, but I cannot tell you anything more than that. I had this information that that kind of meeting had taken place, but after the tragedy in Kravica. Whether this meeting was held then or not, or whether it was held or -- at all or not, I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the information that it was -- it happened in the public security station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I just wanted to ask you, you weren't at that meeting, were you? Obviously not. Okay. Now I want --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- to go back to a document quickly that was covered in part during your cross-examination by my learned friend Mr. -- I'm sorry, Mr. Nikolic. I jumped the gun here. They didn't get your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He needs to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you want, I can restate the question just so it's clear, but you can answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was: "I just wanted to ask you, you weren't at that meeting, were you? Obviously not." Were you at that meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to turn to a document that you looked at yesterday briefly, and that was 1D382. And, sir, you were given a copy, and this is an order dated the 2nd of July, 1995, from the Drina Corps to the Bratunac Brigade. There's a related document, just so the Court has it and we have it in the record, P3025, and you remember the document and the Drina Corps had some handwriting on that document and that you were asked if that was your handwriting, et cetera. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My learned friends from the Office of the Prosecution were kind enough to bring the original document, and I'd like with the Court's permission to tender that document to you and focus your attention specifically on the page where there's evidence in this case that this may be your handwriting, sir, and if you could take a look at that for us one more time just so that the record's clear that you looked at the original document and so we could have your sworn testimony on that. And we're tendering it to the -- Madam Usher, and she will focus your attention on that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. Okay. Okay. [Interpretation] No, this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you seem certain of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to quickly, if I could, again, with the Court's assistance and the assistance of the usher, put this, which is an in-house document that we created after his testimony on this, just to see whether or not his handwriting matches. I know it's not an official handwriting expert, but we wanted to at least get a preliminary -- or have his opinion on that based on at least this preliminary analysis that was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's it, yeah. Oh, yes, please, and show it to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, before we decide on whether to allow you to put this question as you've presented it, what do you mean by "an in-house document we created after his testimony ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I can explain that in detail. Your Honour, after his testimony we were given with the Court's permission his personal notes and records. We didn't learn until his testimony I believe yesterday that he denied this entry on the document from the Drina Corps, and what we did was had a group of the Defence staff look at his handwritten notes and pick out the exact same word and just make a comparison, word underneath word, based on the handwriting that was on the Drina Corps document and those exact words that appear in his handwritten notes that was tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, Mr. Ostojic, in Oric I had counsel stand up and say, You know, my legal assistants - one of the girls who were -- who were working with him - can copy Oric's signature to perfection. Here it is. There is a page with about 10, 20 signatures. So what? Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could just get the original retrieved and returned to the Prosecution so that that chain of custody is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to tell you this because the Court and the rules here suggest that I should put my case to you. We suggest, sir, that that meeting with Mr. Beara where you saw him alone in the middle of the Bratunac centre at 8.00 or 8.30 or whatever time it was on July 13th, 1995, never happened. In fact, we brought evidence, sir, that Mr. Beara was in Belgrade during that time and that the reason, sir, you're not telling us the truth, and I don't mean to insult you, but the reason you're not telling us the truth is because you're bitter and angry at the sentence that you received, and the first time that you ever disclosed any facts in connection with Mr. Beara and these purported meetings and specifically this purported meeting on the 13th of July at 8.00 or 8.30 p.m. was during and after your plea negotiations. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, sir, you have the right to think what you want to think and, of course, to defend your client. What I said, I stand by it. In the statements that I made lies the whole truth. Everything that you said now would be all right, and I would be the happiest man in the world if it hadn't happened, but it did happen. No matter how strongly you try to deny that your client had any role and involvement in all this, I put it to you that the involvement and the responsibility of your client in this operation is ten times that of mine. Why did I accept, and why am I embittered? Of course I am embittered, and I am not trying to hide that, but at the same time I'm also a brave man. Regardless of how this might be difficult for me and the people around me, my family, I really want to tell the truth about who did what and whose role was in this heinous crime, without sparing myself either. If I'm not going to spare myself, then rest assured that I'm not going to spare your client either. There are some other men here who I respect very much, and I am willing to do anything for them. One of those men is Mr. Borovcanin. I would donate blood or my organs to him if necessary. I am not saying that we are the best of friends. We never socialised, but there are people who are honourable and honest officers and the people who enjoy my respect. But they experienced what they experienced, and they have to face the consequences of what had happened to them. I am telling the truth here in the best possible way. Perhaps I'm not very skilful in expressing myself, but I am doing my best to be helpful. I still maintain that everything that happened, and unfortunately, if there hadn't been any victims and if there hadn't been any crime, you could -- could have told to me, Mr. Nikolic, you are lying, you don't know anything. However, the killings took place, and everything happened. Whether it happened one hour earlier or later, whether it happened at 8.00 p.m. or 9.00 p.m. on the 13th is completely irrelevant. I am trying to help the Chamber to arrive at the truth. They should know that a crime had happened, and I shall always be willing to respond to any call from the Trial Chamber. I am very sorry that the OTP perceived my behaviour as hostile, but I was not feeling well. However, I am now feeling well, and I am ready and willing to help the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber in any future proceedings, provided they invite me to do so, of course. And please, I am not embittered against the people who are sitting up there in the dock. I'm only trying to say and describe what I saw and to pass on to you the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Nikolic, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The witness just said on page 68, line 1 and 2, [In English] [Previous translation continues]... continue to have the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. [Interpretation] These are the exact words of the -- of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, if you were so truthful and honest, why didn't you tell the Prosecution prior to your meetings for your plea negotiations any of this evidence you claim you had relating to these purported meetings with Mr. Beara on the 13th of July? Why hadn't you offered that to them in 1999 when you met with them and gave an interview?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999, I simply wasn't ready to talk about any of those things. That was immediately after the war, so four years after the war. The overall situation in Republika Srpska at that time and in the area where I live was terrible. Any statements, any confession of guilt at that time would have been totally unacceptable then, and for the sake of my family and their safety, I didn't want to go down that road. Quite simply, the circumstances were not good for that. People were still losing lives, and I was fearing for my life and the lives of my dearest and nearest. That is why I didn't want to speak about that so soon after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So during these three or four or so meetings that you had with the Prosecution once you wanted to accept and acknowledge your responsibility - although modified, as we've seen - that was the first time that you actually told them about Mr. Beara. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't like to manipulate with this and to commit myself as to when was the first time I spoke about this with the OTP. We had numerous meetings, and I don't want to guess when was the first time that I told the OTP about any event. We went back again and again on -- to certain events. We debated things. We discussed them. Of course there were disagreements. There was lack of understanding because we really talked on numerous occasions about everything, and I can't give you the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just to be fair, the reason I'm asking you, Mr. Nikolic, is because none of those meetings that you had with the Prosecution where you purportedly or seemingly mentioned Mr. Beara, they weren't recorded. There was no transcript of those meetings during your plea negotiations or any of that, and since you were there I thought you might be able to tell me if it happened in the early part, the middle part, or the latter part of your plea negotiations with the Prosecution that you mentioned this alleged encounter with Mr. Beara. But if you don't recall, you -- you can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask you not to insist on this because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you're also aware that Mr. Deronjic pled guilty at or about the same time that you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was a foundational question. Thank you. Did you discuss with Mr. Deronjic at the UNDU his process and his deliberation on seeking to have a plea negotiation with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you something that you probably don't know. I'm not at all close with Miroslav Deronjic regardless of the fact that he had married a cousin of mine. All those who know both of us know that as well. Miroslav Deronjic didn't see me as a person with whom he can talk and confide in, nor did I perceive him in that way. All our conversations were actually short encounters because we were not actually residing in the same part of the unit. Therefore, we never discussed either his agreements with the OTP or my agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you must be aware, Mr. Nikolic, that the first time that Deronjic ever told his tale of this purported meeting with Mr. Beara was just prior to his plea agreement in 2003. And if counsel needs a reference, it's at page 1571; October 28th, 2003. You're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Deronjic's process and negotiations are concerned, I -- I know nothing. I don't know how these negotiations went. I don't know any details involved. I absolutely know nothing because I never had an opportunity to read any document from the -- Deronjic's plea agreement with the exception of the documents provided to me by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm trying to be fair to you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you approaching the end, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am. I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- almost three hours and a half now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, but that's not entirely accurate, and I'm trying to be fair to you, because at your sentencing hearing Mr. Deronjic testified, and here's what was asked. You were present. Here's what was asked on the 28th of October, 2003, at page 1571 by Mr. McCloskey, I believe: To Mr. Deronjic: "Is it fair to say that the first time you ..." I add the parentheses, (Mr. Deronjic) "... told the OTP that Beara had actually talked to you ..." again, parentheses, (Mr. Deronjic) because he's the one who's giving evidence, "... personally about the killing Muslim prisoners was in your recent interviews just prior to the guilty plea?" Answer by Mr. Deronjic, in front of you, sir, while you were there: "Yes, that's correct. That's what I said in my last interview, and he stood by it." You don't remember that at all, that he like you, sir, the first time Mr. Beara's name ever was mentioned despite the prior interviews or contacts you had with the Office of the Prosecution and this tale that you and Mr. Deronjic created was only during your plea negotiation in order for you to get a lighter sentence; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't want to comment the statements made by Mr. Deronjic at all. I don't want to make any comments on that. I can only comment my statements and what I wrote down. I cannot and I do not wish to make comments about anyone's statement why he said what he said and why he did what he did. My statement is what you heard from me today, and I stand by it. You can interpret in any way you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I based on the time constraints will stop here, but I did have several other areas that I could address with the Court after the witness finishes that I would have liked to ask the witness questions on, specifically, that comment I see from my notes, are the Dragomir Vasic documents where he describes the role of the civilian police in both Potocari, Bratunac, and Zvornik, but I'm adhering to the Court's ruling, and I'll have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you prefer to start immediately, Ms. Nikolic, or do you wish to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it would be more appropriate to have a break now and give some time to Mr. Nikolic to recuperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we have 25 minutes' break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw you standing, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to thank the Court for giving me the additional time that you did, and it's very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very nice of you to say that. Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My name is Jelena Nikolic. I appear on behalf of Mr. Drago Nikolic. It means that there are four Nikolics in this courtroom alone.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, it seems that there's very many of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a good sign. I mean, my surname in Malta accounts to something like 50.000 people, and that's -- it has always been a positive sign to me. We are prolific.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in order for the two of us to understand each other well, since we speak the same language, I will caution you and myself to wait to finish each other's questions and answers so that we could have an accurate transcript. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 22nd of April, 2009, when you were being examined by my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic, you said that among the officers of the Zvornik Brigade you knew Drago Nikolic. Can you tell me, how long did you know him and in what way, personally or professionally?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Drago Nikolic as a person who hails from the same municipality as I do. Privately speaking, we did not socialise. We did not know each other, had any contact of that type. In our official capacities, we seldom met, barely ever, during the war, save for accidental meetings at the corps command at this or that meeting, but it was seldom. Nothing in particular to say. Nothing official, I'd say. I knew him as a person born in the village of Kravica, that he resided there and had family. That was the extent of me and Drago Nikolic's acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And I suppose you know Mr. Nikolic's family from Kravica, at least by sight?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean his immediate family, I don't. I may have seen them or met him -- met them, but I don't think I know Drago Nikolic's immediate family members. The Nikolic family in Kravica is a large one, and most of them I know by sight, and some of them even personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Nikolic's parents and brothers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw them on occasion, but I didn't pay much heed. I did not have any contact with any members of his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the 13th of July, 1995, did you on occasion go to the Zvornik Brigade, to any meetings with the security organ there, Mr. Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise. I don't know which period you have in mind exactly, but what I can recall best is that on one occasion I was in the Zvornik Brigade to attend a workshop or training session. I am not sure. In any case, I can confirm to you that at least on one occasion I went to the offices of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go to July 1995 next, the period between the 11th of that month and the following days. Did you have any telephone or other type of communication with the Zvornik Brigade or Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that there was no communication with Drago Nikolic. I did not see him in the course of those few days, as regards the Bratunac Brigade, that is, and the part that has to do with Bratunac and Srebrenica. I'm positive we did not speak over the phone, Drago Nikolic and I, or anyone else from the Zvornik Brigade, for that matter. I don't think there were any conversations before that either, because there was no need for me to contact them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we may conclude that in the period between the 11th and the 13th of July, you did not see Drago Nikolic in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I didn't see him in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As of the 13th of July, and I mean July, August, September, you did not have any contact with Drago Nikolic by phone or any other way, and I mean 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to talk about your alleged conversation with Drago Nikolic at the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade in the night of the 13th of July, 1995. You have testified extensively about that, and I will not go back to the details. At page 32 -- 937, lines 20 to 23 you explained to the Chamber what the context was of the message you conveyed to Drago Nikolic, that is to say that the people who had been separated and kept in Bratunac were to be transferred to Zvornik, and that it was his task to have the location ready to receive the prisoners. You referred to it in similar terms in the Trbic case, but I would like to quote that part of the text to you and then put a question. For my learned friends, it is P4482, page 25 in the B/C/S; in the English, 63. In answering Mr. Trbojevic's [phoen] question you said: Yes, that's how it was. That's what I told Drago, that I had information that the people who had been captured and who were going to be transferred to Zvornik, that they would be killed. That's what I told him, meaning that was the information I had. That is what I knew, and that was my assessment. I shared that with him. Defence: Did he anything say concerning your remark? Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: neither commented the arrival of the prisoners nor anything of what I told him. He said very well, Nidzo. You conveyed the order, and I simply did not offer any further comment. Do you recall this, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Given Drago Nikolic's reaction as you described it in the Trbic case, he was quite taken aback by the message you conveyed to him.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to confirm that what you said more or less was what I told him on that occasion. Of course he was surprised, and I can confirm that because I'm being asked of that. He was surprised because I suppose until that point he wasn't aware of what was going on and what was to be the further stages of the operation. What you read basically fully accurately reflects Drago Nikolic's reaction at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Given your answer about his surprised reaction, you were able to conclude that you were the first person to tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't thinking about whether I was the first person to tell him that or not. However, I do suppose that I was the first person to convey to him the message that those captured in Bratunac were to be transferred to the area of the Zvornik Brigade. I suppose I was the first person to tell him that. Whether he had any other knowledge or not, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your conversation with Drago was a brief one, as you testified, five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even that long. It was very brief. I did not enter the forward command post building, and I had no other business there. I came there, turned my car around, got out, told him that, got back into the car with the policeman and left. It may have lasted five, six, or seven minutes at the most, or perhaps ten, not even.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will go back to these details later. I would like to answer the following: What you said in the Blagojevic case as well as in the Trbic case, the portion I just read out to you, as well as the things you said to the Bench here today, that is fully accurate of what you and Drago Nikolic spoke about that day. There was nothing beyond that that Drago Nikolic told you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that's correct. Perhaps there may have been one sentence in a testimony or a statement of mine, and that is that before I got back in the car Drago told me that he was to see with his command what was to follow, what to do with what I told him. That was the only sentence extra, and Drago and I did not discuss this or any other matter later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Drago therefore never mentioned to you that he had information that the captured people were to come to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I never said so. That was how the conversation developed. That was our first and last encounter. We never saw each other after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic never told you that he had allegedly spoken with Colonel Popovic or Obrenovic on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw him?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I don't remember ever having said anything similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And, of course, on the 13th of July you never told Drago Nikolic that the Zvornik Brigade was supposed to execute those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I said and the way you read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Including that the Zvornik Brigade was supposed to carry out the executions of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it because I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After that, you left the area.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After your departure, during that night Drago remained at the forward command post; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the moment of your departure ...

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about that moment, then, yes, Drago Nikolic stayed at that place where I had found him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He did not go back with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Nikolic, please try not to overlap. Just allow a brief pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now a few general questions concerning the relationship between the military police and the security organ. You discussed that during Mr. Thayer's examination, as well as in your previous testimonies. Did you command the MP platoon in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you issue direct orders to them in July 1995 and to Mirko Jankovic who was the MP platoon commander in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly, no, I did not issue orders to the MP commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In which way did you do it, then, and what was the relationship between the security organ and the military police in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Direct command and control of the military police, since you're asking about command, is in the hands of an officer of the unit within which the MP unit is per establishment or attached to. Speaking in the military professional terms, an MP platoon or military police in general is controlled by the security organ, in professional terms. This does not entail direct and immediate issuance of orders. The commander of the unit within which the MP unit is contained is the only person, the only officer who can issue orders to the military police through their MP platoon commander, and to military policemen directly, it can only be done by the MP platoon commander. He can issues direct tasks to them. In professional terms, professional control means equipping, training, and following the state of combat readiness of that unit. The security organ, among other things, is tasked with taking care of the readiness of the MP unit at any point in time so as to be at the full disposal of the commander of the unit attached to. In brief, that would be the relationship between the military police and the security organ. If you're interested in anything else, please ask me and I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As a security organ, if you needed to use the military police for a specific task, were you allowed to single out policemen and take them to carry out this task, or did you have to seek approval from their commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able, and I did take part in making proposals to the commander about the ways in which he should use the military police. That is one of the tasks of a security organ. But, of course, before the commander makes a decision how to use the military police, it was no place for me to take a decision, to pick ten policemen and take them into the field. That is to say, pursuant to the decision made by the commander to use a unit for a specific task, the unit commander and the commander of the military police decides the schedule, decides the size and the composition of the unit, and from the professional point of view, if it is necessary to have cooperation with the security organ, then he would seek such cooperation. And if the security organ, vice versa, decides that he should offer assistance, then he should be the one to provide this professional assistance to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you one more question about these general matters relating to your job as the security organ. How independent were you as a security organ of the brigade in discharging your duties, and in what aspects?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a difference between what I did and what Mr. Drago Nikolic did. I was a security intelligence organ with a Light Infantry Brigade, whereas Drago Nikolic was a security chief in the Infantry Brigade, and these two functions are separate. Now, again I'm not saying this affirmatively, but I think that I can say that Drago Nikolic was an authorised official, whereas I wasn't. That's the difference. Mr. Drago was in charge of security issues, and he was authorised to do that. I, on the other hand, was in charge of intelligence and security affairs, and the focus of my engagement was intelligence, and I was only in charge of security at the command staff, and that refers only to providing protection of one's own unit. Therefore, in any criminal proceedings I couldn't appear as an authorised official who could file criminal reports, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All I wanted to ask you is the following: Were you involved in counter-intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you act independently in that area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In applying the methods of works?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in that area. When you speak about counter-intelligence, my job was to make assessments regarding the enemy. I'm not particularly skilled, and my expertise is not significant there. I just made assessments about the enemy, their intentions, and things like that. As for the application of the methods of intelligence, security organs, you have to apply rules which also on the other hand implies seeking certain permissions, and in that sense the security organ is not independent. If they want to apply these methods, they need to seek approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. From this I understand that security of the brigade was not your primary task, and you don't feel to be fully qualified to do that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I wouldn't like to make any comments on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going too fast, and you're overlapping again. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I apologise on your behalf as well.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to do my best because I sometimes forget about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let us now move to another area. When you answered questions asked by Mr. Zivanovic about the officers you knew in the Zvornik Brigade, you said that you knew only a few of them. So can we please now have in e-court Exhibit P2880. You will see in front of you, Mr. Nikolic, a photograph, and I'd like to ask you, are you familiar with the officers by the name Nenad Simic; Dusko Vukotic; Mico Petkovic, assistant of the chief of staff for intelligence and moral guidance; Sreten Milosevic, assistant for logistics? Do you recognise any of the people in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you positively that I recognise two people only, Mr. Pandurevic -- Pandurevic and Drago. I may have seen the others at some point, but believe me, I wouldn't remember any single name. I heard of Vukotic and some other names, but I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Have you ever met Sreten Milosevic in 1996, in 1997, in the printing house in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I was the manager of that printing plant, and it is possible, but please believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps recognise him in this photo? This was taken in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I really cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can remove this document from the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to your statement of facts. That's 4D16, item 10. You testified at length about the meeting in Bratunac during Mr. Ostojic's cross-examination. However, can we establish as a fact from 6th of May, 2003, when you signed this statement, that at around 2030 hours after the alleged meeting in Bratunac with Colonel Beara, you set off to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At that point, you were told that you were going to the Zvornik Brigade command in Karakaj to see Drago Nikolic and to convey personally Colonel Beara's message to him.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore, at that point when you set off for Zvornik, what you knew was that Drago was probably at the Zvornik Brigade command in Karakaj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And no one had any information, neither you nor Colonel Beara, that he was actually at the forward command post, which we only learned later.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say for myself I didn't have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Having read your testimony in the Blagojevic case, it seems that you were then able to provide more details to the Chamber. You said, for example, that the distance between Bratunac and Zvornik was 42 kilometres, that it was dusk or early evening. Can you tell us what was the situation on the road? Was the road blocked? At which route did you take while driving?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I passed there, control points had already been erected in Kravica, in Konjevic Polje, and also in front of Kuslac. There was a sort of check-point on the road as well. There was one in the Drinjaca sector. There were a number of people in uniforms. I don't know if they were military or police. And that is all that I saw on that road, and I travelled from Bratunac via Kravica, Konjevic Polje, and Drinjaca. And it is true that the distance is -- to Zvornik is about 42 kilometres, and I don't know how far the command itself from that point is. Let's say two or three kilometres more because the command headquarters is outside of town. It was July, so it was not night-time. It was 8.00 or 8.30 in the evening. So that's -- I would call that early evening or dusk.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As you said in your testimony in the Blagojevic case, your ride took about one hour.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking. I didn't have any problems or -- or difficulties on the road. I just said hello to people in Konjevic Polje, people from Bratunac who were manning that check-point, and I just proceeded on my way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what vehicle did you use? Was anyone else with you in this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was alone, and I think I drove a Golf car.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was that a civilian vehicle or a military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a civilian vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: With civilian licence plates or military licence plates?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. It belonged to the VRS, the Bratunac Brigade. It had been mobilised and was in the possession of the brigade. It was given to me for use.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: According to item 1 of your statement of facts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Item 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In 2003, you said that you arrived at the Zvornik Brigade at around 21.45.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said that, I can repeat now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you, had you announced your arrival to the Zvornik Brigade? Did you contact them from any point before you set off?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you came outside the gate to the Zvornik Brigade, you stopped at the gatehouse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I'm going to show you now this gate. So please, if we can see in e-court Exhibit 3D502, which is the gatehouse or the gate to the barracks of the Zvornik Brigade. Mr. Nikolic, in front of you, you can see this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would kindly ask the usher to give a pencil to Mr. Nikolic so that he can mark the place where he parked his car.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you recognise this photograph? Do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. This is -- this used to be a factory before the war, one of the factories in Zvornik. During the war, it was converted to the Zvornik Brigade command headquarters. What I see here, if I see it correctly, at the entrance to the Zvornik Brigade command headquarters is a little office, and this is the direction when you move from Zvornik towards Karakaj, what I'm showing to you now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark this direction with the pencil so that I can see that on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say if this is direction from Zvornik to Karakaj, then the Zvornik Brigade building is on the right-hand side, and at the entrance there's the gatehouse or the little office where the duty officer sits. I stopped immediately in front of the Zvornik Brigade command, that is to say outside the asphalt road of the road that leads to Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please put a number 1 on the spot where you stopped your car.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly. Let's say here in front of the gatehouse, or maybe a little bit further on. I really cannot tell you exactly. This will be roughly the place where I stopped the car. Anyway, it was not in the road lane or the road leading to Karakaj. This is the office which I approached, and I reported to the people who were manning the gatehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. This is where you stopped, and you marked it with number 1. Was there any gate or swinging barrier at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was the gate closed or was the --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was closed, and the only way in was here where the office is. Let me just add one thing. You're asking me about these details, and I really try to answer your questions to the best of my ability, but I really didn't pay attention to these details that you're asking me about, whether the gate was closed, whether the swinging barrier was up or down. But nevertheless, I will try to tell you everything that I know that you request me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please don't expect me to be very precise because I didn't pay attention to these details at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you came to the gatehouse - you already told Mr. Zivanovic, and I do not intend to go into that again - you produced your ID, which is not an official one, is that right, and you explained that you were looking for Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers or military policemen were there as you approached the reception area, the reception booth at the gate to the brigade HQ? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the booth there were two individuals outside of it, and within the reception booth there were two to three individuals. I'm not quite sure. There were at least two of them inside and a group of people -- a group of soldiers in uniform outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, there were persons around the reception booth?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did they allow you to enter the compound in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't attempt to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did you park your vehicle, then?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I reported to the gate, I proceeded to a car parking across the road from the brigade HQ, left -- parked the car there and went back through the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did the military policemen enter your name into the log of visitors, the ones who were manning the reception booth as you entered the gate?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I gave them the ID I had containing all my personal details. I told them that I was a security organ from the Bratunac Brigade. Whether they copied my details somewhere, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From the reception booth, from the gate to the brigade building, did you pass that particular distance alone or with someone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an individual, whether he was a military policeman or somebody else, who escorted me into the building and on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to draw the two circles on the photograph, to put number 1 and place the date and your initials at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say? What am I supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the lower right-hand corner, or left-hand corner, whatever you prefer, place the date and your initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
